Quantifying Geographic Accessibility to Optimize Entomological Surveillance Site Selection in Kasaï-Central, DRC

A project proposal for MAP Early Career Researcher (ECR) study

Authors
Affiliations

Victoire Nsabatien

The Kids Research Institute Australia

Arsene Bokulu

Institut National de la Recherche Biomédicale (INRB)

Kaiza Ilomo

Ifakara Health Institute

Published

July 15, 2026

Abstract

Malaria vector surveillance in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) depends on a sparse network of sentinel village sites that are costly to reach and maintain. This proposal sets out a geospatial project to quantify geographic accessibility — travel time to candidate sites — and combine it with vector density and human-settlement indicators to make surveillance site selection more efficient, more representative, and more affordable. Building on a province-wide entomological dataset collected during the Victoire’s PhD in Kasaï-Central, the project will produce provincial travel-time surfaces, a quadrant prioritisation framework (accessibility × vector density), and practical planning tools for the NMCP. The proposal is scoped as an ECR study intended for peer-reviewed publication.

1 Background and rationale

Malaria remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and the National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) relies on entomological surveillance to track vector species composition, abundance, and behaviour. Surveillance is organised through sentinel village sites where vectors are sampled longitudinally. Because DRC is vast and its road network is sparse and often seasonal, the cost of reaching and servicing a site — and the practicality of training and supervising field teams — is dominated by geographic accessibility, i.e. travel time across the landscape rather than straight-line distance.

Site selection today is largely driven by convenience and historical precedent rather than by an explicit trade-off between how informative a site is (the vector dynamics it captures) and how reachable it is (the operational cost to monitor it). This creates two risks: hard-to-reach but epidemiologically important areas are under-sampled, while easy-to-reach but low-value sites absorb scarce resources.

DRC’s health system is administratively nested — province → health zone (zone de santé) → health area (aire de santé) → village — which gives a natural hierarchy for both sampling design and decision-making. Health areas are each served by a health centre, and the number of areas within a zone scales roughly with population density.

This project asks whether quantifying geographic accessibility can improve the efficiency of malaria vector surveillance in DRC, using the province of Kasaï-Central as a case study. Victoire collected an entomological dataset across this province as part of his PhD (26 health zones; sampling in one health area / village per zone; 25 households per village; 12 months of collection), which provides per-village species counts to anchor the analysis.

Note

This proposal is a new, standalone study distinct from Victoire’s PhD. It is intended to be developed with ECR mentors and partners toward a peer-reviewed publication, with NMCP as the primary end user.

2 Study setting

The study is set in the DRC, one of 26 provinces of which is Kasaï-Central, where Victoire’s fieldwork was conducted (Figure 1).

Within Kasaï-Central the health system comprises 25 health zones, roughly 442–466 health areas, and about 4,856 villages (Figure 2). This nested structure is the spatial backbone for the accessibility and sampling analyses.

Table 1 summarises the health areas and villages per health zone, based on the Victoire’s compiled data.

3 Aim and research questions

Overall aim: to quantify geographic accessibility across Kasaï-Central and use it — together with vector density and human-settlement indicators — to optimise the selection and operation of entomological surveillance sites.

The proposal consolidates several related ideas into one core question with optional extensions:

Primary research question

Can geographic accessibility improve the efficiency of malaria vector surveillance site selection?

Secondary / extension questions

  1. Network sizing. How many surveillance sites are actually needed to capture vector dynamics while minimising operational cost and travel time?
  2. Settlement as a predictor. Do building-footprint metrics improve predictions of Anopheles occurrence and abundance beyond environmental variables alone?
  3. Transmission-opportunity mapping. Does combining a mosquito-breeding layer with a human-exposure layer produce more accurate maps of transmission opportunity than either alone?
  4. Training logistics. How much travel time and operational cost can be reduced through accessibility-based planning of program activities such as field-team training?

4 Objectives

  1. Build provincial travel-time surfaces to candidate sentinel village sites using open geospatial layers (roads, land cover, hydrology, terrain) and established accessibility-modelling methods.
  2. Cross the accessibility surface with per-village vector density to derive a quadrant prioritisation framework for site selection.
  3. Propose a stratified sampling design that identifies the most efficient locations for longitudinal entomological data collection.
  4. (Extension) Evaluate building footprints as a predictor of vector occurrence/abundance and as a human-exposure layer.
  5. (Extension) Develop an accessibility-based training-logistics tool that tells each zone/area/village the nearest feasible training location.

5 Conceptual framework: accessibility × vector density

The analytically richest output cross-references the travel-time surface with per-village species counts to place every candidate site into one of four quadrants (Table 2). This turns two continuous surfaces into an actionable decision rule.

6 Data sources

  • Administrative & population boundaries and health facilities: GRID3 DRC geospatial data (provinces, health zones, health areas, villages, health facilities) — see grid3.org/geospatial-data-drc.
  • Entomological data: Victoire’s province-wide dataset (per-village Anopheles species counts; 26 health zones; 25 households/village; 12 months).
  • Building footprints / settlement: Google Open Buildings V2 (Figure 4).
  • Environmental & accessibility covariates: land cover, roads, hydrology, topography, rainfall, and vegetation indices from open sources.

Figure 3 shows the existing health-facility network — the practical service and access points that anchor travel-time origins and training venues.

7 Methods

7.1 Accessibility (travel-time) modelling

Construct a friction surface from land cover, road class, slope, and hydrology, then compute least-cost travel time from population centres and health facilities to candidate sentinel sites (and vice versa). Produce preliminary provincial maps of travel time to candidate village sites for each health zone, enabling the NMCP to compare candidate sites on a like-for-like accessibility basis.

7.2 Vector-density integration and prioritisation

Interpolate/aggregate the per-village species counts to the health-area level and overlay them on the travel-time surface to populate the quadrant framework (Table 2). Identify and rank monitoring sites where pre-intervention vector densities are predicted to be high and accessibility is favourable.

7.3 Stratified sampling design

Use the combined accessibility and density surfaces to propose a stratified sampling scheme, and estimate the minimum number of sites required to capture provincial vector dynamics within acceptable precision — directly addressing the network-sizing question.

7.4 Building footprints and vector distribution (extension)

Because host availability drives biting opportunity, building-footprint density is a plausible proxy for human population and therefore for where host-seeking vectors concentrate (Figure 4). Test whether building-footprint metrics improve models of Anopheles occurrence/abundance beyond environmental covariates, and use them to flag health areas within each zone that the NMCP might prioritise for vector-control tools.

7.5 Transmission-opportunity mapping (extension)

Combine a mosquito-breeding layer (water, hydrology, topography, rainfall, vegetation) with a human-exposure layer (building footprints, population, settlement density) to classify areas (Table 3).

Working hypothesis: building footprints capture vector–host encounter opportunities while larval-habitat suitability captures mosquito production; combining both yields more accurate maps of malaria-transmission opportunity than either approach alone.

7.6 Training-logistics optimisation (extension)

During PhD fieldwork, field teams were grouped into training pools by accessibility rather than by administrative tidiness — e.g. teams reached the Demba pool more easily from Kalomba and Ndekesha than from Bilomba, because of distance and road quality (Figure 5). Formalising this, the travel-time model can assign each zone/area/village to its nearest feasible training venue, reducing travel time and cost for program activities such as entomological and epidemiological training.

8 Expected outputs

  • Provincial travel-time surfaces and per-zone accessibility maps.
  • A quadrant prioritisation of candidate sentinel sites.
  • A stratified sampling design with an estimate of the minimum viable number of surveillance sites.
  • (Extension) Evidence on building footprints as a vector-occurrence predictor and transmission-opportunity maps.
  • (Extension) An accessibility-based training-logistics planning tool.
  • One or more peer-reviewed manuscripts and NMCP-facing decision aids.

9 Significance

For the NMCP and funders, the outputs convert scattered field knowledge into explicit, defensible decisions: where to place sentinel sites, how many are enough, which health areas to prioritise for vector-control tools, and where to hold training to minimise cost. The approach is transferable to other DRC provinces and to comparable resource-limited settings.

10 Next steps

Immediate next steps are to (1) confirm scope and lead research question with mentors, (2) assemble the open geospatial layers and the entomological dataset, and (3) produce a first provincial travel-time surface for one health zone as a proof of concept.

11 Key reference

Weiss et al. and related accessibility work motivate the core method; the directly relevant methodological reference is Quantifying geographic accessibility to improve efficiency of entomological monitoring (bioRxiv 10.1101/779561v2).
